newsitem.title: MEXICO: China cutting excess steel inventories - IISI.
newsitem.headline: China cutting excess steel inventories - IISI.

text.p: China is currently still cutting down steel inventories through either absorbing them into the production chain or re-exporting, the secretary- general of the International Iron and Steel Institute said here Monday.

Speaking at the Latin American Steel Congress here in northern Mexico, Lenhard Holschuh said Chinese apparent consumption levels had gone down as a result, but forecast an upturn next year returning to levels around 100 million tonnes per year.
"This is another region where inventories of steel have caused massive distortion in the pattern of apparent consumption," Holschuh said.

"In 1993 and 1994, China imported (a combined total of) 62 million tonnes of finished and semi-finished steel, and exported less than 4 million tonnes. Apparent consumption jumped sharply, but a lot of this material was bought speculatively and ended up swelling inventories held within the country," he added.

"Through 1995 and 1996, these excess inventories have been absorbed into the production chain, or re-exported at very depressed levels, depressing apparent consumption...but by 1997 this problem will have been resolved, and apparent consumption will return to 100 million tonnes, in line with the level of real consumption in China," he said.

Holschuh said trade flows were a destabilising factor for world steel markets. "China had net imports of 23 million tonnes in 1994, then in 1995, imports dropped by 10 million tonnes and exports jumped by 8 million tonnes," he said.

"This turnaround meant that almost 3 percent of world's total output of steel products was looking for additional export market in 1995 and this was probably the biggest single factor underlying the deflation of world markets in 1995," Holschuh concluded.
